data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The safest protocol is an append-only intent-and-seal log with epoch fencing; it dominates lease-based alternatives because it records causality directly rather than inferring it from timeouts, and the exact durable records are the intent entry and the seal entry.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The log is subject to unbounded growth if seal records are never compacted","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the log service is partitioned, the protocol stalls rather than reclaims","eval":"observation"},{"case":"A process that writes an intent but crashes before touching the workspace creates a phantom reclamation candidate that wastes space until TTL","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Before acquiring the workspace, the process appends an intent record (problem_id, epoch, workspace_path, process_id) to a durable append-only log. Upon completion, it appends a seal record containing the output evidence hash. Reclamation performs a log-scan: any workspace with an intent but no matching seal, whose holding process has been confirmed dead by a liveness oracle, is reclaimed. The causal mechanism is that the log provides a recoverable total order of intent and seal events, so displacement is always preceded by a visible gap (intent without seal), never silent. Adjudication against lease protocols: where the evidence shows lease expiry can race with seal writes, the log protocol wins because seal visibility is immediate to readers of the log, whereas lease expiry is a timeout inference.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
